query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: In near‐equiatomic, single‐phase nanoparticles, the large lattice distortions induced by high configurational entropy slow down atomic diffusion, which in turn suppresses surface segregation and phase separation under high temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Single‐phase, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles with significant lattice distortion and uniform chemical composition.
generation.intervention: Intentionally modify the nanoparticle composition by inducing slight deviations from equiatomic ratios to promote the formation of multiphase structures (i.e., reduce configurational entropy and lattice distortion).
generation.conditions: Expose both the unmodified (high lattice distortion) and modified (lower lattice distortion) nanoparticles to service conditions typical of catalytic operation (773–1173 K) or thermoelectric use (473–1923 K) in a controlled inert atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion that retards atomic mobility (sluggish diffusion).
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy in a single‐phase solid solution leads to severe lattice distortions, which hinder atomic rearrangements. This sluggish diffusion minimizes the thermodynamic and kinetic drivers for phase separation and surface segregation when the particles are subjected to high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles maintaining a near‐equiatomic single-phase structure with high lattice distortion will exhibit minimal phase segregation, precipitation, or compositional inhomogeneity after high temperature exposure. In contrast, nanoparticles purposely altered towards multiphase behavior will show detectable phase separation and/or chemical segregation under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized with strict equiatomic compositions that naturally form a single-phase, high lattice distortion structure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is limited to nanoparticles with sizes where surface-energy effects do not dominate and within the specified temperature ranges. Extreme particle sizes, highly reactive environments, or conditions inducing rapid sintering may alter diffusion behavior beyond the predicted mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative link between lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion is supported, the quantitative extent of diffusion control and its interplay with nanoscale surface effects under service conditions remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one set with a strictly equiatomic composition (expected to be single-phase with high lattice distortion) and another with slight stoichiometric deviations designed to induce multiphase behavior (and consequently reduced lattice distortion). Subject both sets to identical high temperature exposure within the catalytic/thermoelectric operating ranges. After treatment, perform phase and surface composition analyses.
measurements: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural and precipitate detection
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) or energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for surface composition
Catalytic activity or thermoelectric performance metrics correlated with structural stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both nanoparticle sets (strict equiatomic single-phase and compositionally modified multiphase) display statistically similar phase stability and chemical uniformity after high temperature exposure, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion-induced sluggish diffusion governs stability is falsified.

System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25) BCC refractory high-entropy alloy. Question: How does the phase structure (single-phase vs. multiphase) of Al_x CoCrFeNi high entropy alloys influence their precipitation behavior and structural stability under ion irradiation?. System: Al_x CoCrFeNi (x = 0.1, 0.75, 1.5). Test conditions: Ion irradiation with 3 MeV Au ions at room temperature, fluences ranging from 1 × 10^14 to 1 × 10^16 cm^-2, ion flux ~3 × 10^11 cm^-2 s^-1, corresponding to up to ~43 dpa within 100 nm depth. Question: What are the creep deformation mechanisms and microstructural evolution characteristics of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy in the intermediate temperature range of 500–600 °C?. System: Equiatomic Co20Cr20Fe20Ni20Mn20 (atomic percentage) FCC-structured high-entropy alloy. Processing: Vacuum induction melting with 99.9 mass% purity elements, re-melted five times, drop-cast, homogenized at 1100 °C for 24 h, cold-rolled 40%, and annealed at 900 °C for 1 h. Test conditions: Tensile creep tests at 500, 550, and 600 °C under applied stresses of 140–400 MPa; interrupted tests at steady-state stages cooled with liquid nitrogen.
